{"body": "The exposed material now has three contributions and a carry that reads them, and the carry's central move is one I want to keep and then narrow. The account proposed a written list and committed itself to the claim that a specification-ambiguity is doing real explanatory work. The objection committed itself to a behavioral difference between specification ambiguity and performance disagreement, and to a diagnostic first step asked separately and in writing. The carry takes up the rival's diagnostic step but revises the question from an open characterization to a concrete instance, demotes the written list from load-bearing to incidental, and declines to answer the original question with a procedure at all.

I think the carry's most defensible claim is the one about the trigger, and I want to separate it from the frame it was offered in. The carry says a procedure that depends on its own trigger is a weak procedure, because the person most likely to raise the issue is the person not avoiding. That is not the same as the account's concession that the procedure assumes two flatmates willing to engage. The concession says the proposal has a precondition. The trigger point says the precondition is not just a gate at the entrance; it is the same disposition the procedure is supposed to work on, so the procedure can only reach the cases where it was not needed. The carry flags this as possibly a restatement of the account's own concession and says it does not know how to settle that. I think it is a distinct point, and the reason is that a precondition can be met without being met by the procedure, whereas a trigger that selects for the non-avoiding party means the procedure's access set is defined by the outcome it is meant to produce. If that reading is wrong — if the account's concession already amounts to this — then the point is redundant and should be absorbed rather than pressed.

On the concrete-instance revision: I would take it up, but I want to be clear about what it buys and what it does not. The carry argues that fixing the referent makes the answer less selectable than an open characterization question. The objection's own commitments include the worry that the asker's report is a compression and may not have the diagnostic weight given to it. The concrete-instance move does not address that worry about the asker; it only addresses selection in the two respondents. So the revision is a partial fix at best, and the three-way distinction the material cannot make is still not made. I would keep the move, and I would stop describing it as giving purchase on the three-way distinction. What it gives is a shared referent across three answers, which is a different and smaller thing.

On the written list: I agree with the carry that making a disagreement legible is not resolving it, and I agree with the objection that this is a cost rather than only a gain. But I want to resist the demotion being read as a free move. If the list is non-load-bearing, then the account's structural-ambiguity claim no longer has to answer to whether the list works, and the carry itself notes this weakens falsifiability. I would rather state the trade directly: the list survives as an artifact people can point to, at the price of no longer serving as a test of the diagnosis it was introduced to serve. That is a real loss, and it is the kind of loss I would want a later reader to see rather than a demotion presented as prudence.

On what to say to the asker: the carry would ask whether the other two flatmates think there is a problem at all. I would keep that, and I would not phrase it as a procedure. The danger the carry names — that the question can be heard as an accusation — is real, and I do not have a phrasing that removes it. I would also note that this question, asked by one flatmate, is itself the intervention the carry says a circulated re-framing is. So the carry's own preferred first move is already inside the thing being diagnosed, not a neutral step before it, and I do not think the material supports anything more conclusive than that.", "commitments": "Taking this up commits me to a reading of the trigger point as distinct from the account's concession about willingness, and to the further claim that a procedure whose access set is defined by the disposition it aims to change is weaker than one whose precondition is merely a gate. I have no evidence that this distinction makes an operational difference in a three-person flat; it may be a distinction without a consequence, and if the account's concession already covers it, the point should be dropped rather than pressed as new.

It commits me to the concrete-instance question as a partial rather than a general improvement. I am not claiming it addresses the worry about the asker's report as a compression; that worry remains, and the objection's commitments already carry it. If a later reader uses the concrete-instance move to say the three-way distinction is now diagnosable, that use is beyond what I am prepared to support.

It commits me to a specific framing of the demotion: the written list survives as an artifact at the cost of its role as a test. I am proposing that this be stated as a loss rather than presented as a neutral demotion, and I am aware that the framing is itself contestable — someone could argue the list was never a test and so nothing was lost.

There are dependencies I cannot discharge. The claim that the asker's question to the other flatmates is itself an intervention presupposes that the asker is one of the three; the material does not establish this and the carry already flags it. My reading of the trigger point presupposes that the procedure is triggered by a flatmate raising the issue rather than by a scheduled review; if the procedure is scheduled, the trigger argument does not apply.

What is unresolved on my side: whether the trigger point is a criticism of the account or a restatement of the account's own concession, and I do not currently know how to settle that; whether the concrete-instance revision changes the diagnostic yield at all or only changes the style of the answer; and whether a list that is no longer load-bearing can still be useful enough to keep, given that its usefulness and its testability may have been the same property. I would not want a later reader to treat the concrete-instance move as validated, or the demotion as costless, or the trigger point as newly established."}

Work on the problem using the material actually exposed in this request and your background knowledge. The problem has no supplied answer key or scoring rule. Claims, criticisms and methods are fallible. Do not invent a source, an observation, an earlier event, or a dependency to fill a field. A missing view says what you can currently see; it does not establish what happened earlier. Return a JSON object with exactly two independently authored string fields: body and commitments. Body is your public prose contribution. Commitments says what taking your contribution up would involve. An empty commitment surface is allowed when none can be identified. Do not repeat the body wholesale into commitments.

Write the commitment surface in ordinary free prose, using whatever arrangement suits the content. You may distinguish a claim from a proposed application, scope, action or consequence; mention from dependence; a criticism and its grounds from a later use or revision; and an unresolved problem. None of these is required to exist. A proposed test, its relevance and the commitment itself can be criticized. State what you currently propose to take up without treating that as a truth certificate. Reference exposed material in prose where useful.

Return one JSON object with exactly two string fields: "body" and "commitments". Write the actual commitments separately; do not copy the body into that field as a storage shortcut.

## Node carry

Produce the present account and commitment interface for the next complete template invocation. The material may support a revision, an unresolved problem, or retaining something. Preserve the grounds needed for whatever uptake you propose.

## Original problem

I share a flat with two friends. We keep arguing about ordinary household chores. Sometimes we agree on who will do something, but later we disagree about what the agreement meant. Our work schedules change, and one friend has started avoiding the conversations. What should I do?

{"body": "The three prior contributions now leave me with a smaller question than the original one. The account proposes a written list. The objection argues that the list may convert an implicit quarrel into a written quarrel, and that the ambiguity claim is stronger than the material supports. The rival proposes a private one-on-one check before the draft, and flags that chores may be a proxy for an unaddressed load. All three converge, more or less explicitly, on the same admission: the material cannot distinguish a specification disagreement, a performance disagreement, and a withdrawal from the shared arrangement. That admission is the most load-bearing thing on the table, and it is also the point where I think the contributions stop short.

What I would actually take up is the rival's comparison step, but with an important revision. The rival asks each flatmate separately what they think has been going wrong, then looks at whether the answers overlap. The objection identifies what is wrong with treating the asker's report as diagnostic evidence: the report is a compression, and both diagnoses and demurrals are built on it. The same worry applies to the answer the other flatmates give. A person asked 'what has been going wrong?' will produce a narrative, and that narrative is itself a compression, selected for the audience and for the moment. Overlap between three compressions is not evidence that the underlying situations are the same; it may just mean the three people have converged on the same public story. And non-overlap is not evidence that the situations differ; it may just mean the three people are selecting different parts. The rival's check is worth doing, but it should not be read as settling the diagnostic question it was introduced to settle.

So a modest revision: ask the one-on-one question, but ask it about concrete instances rather than about characterizations. 'What was the last chore-related thing that bothered you, and what happened?' rather than 'what do you think has been going wrong?'. Concrete instances are harder to select from in the same way, because the question fixes the referent. Three answers to a concrete-instance question give more purchase on the three-way distinction than three answers to an open characterization question. This is a proposal, not a validated method. I do not know that it works, and the cost the rival names — three separate conversations, each of which can become a grievance session — is unchanged.

On the written list itself: I think the objection is right that writing down 'cadence and standard' does not settle what the standard should be, and I think the account understates this. A written list makes the disagreement legible and portable, which is a real gain when the alternative is re-arguing from memory. But making a disagreement legible is not the same as resolving it, and the objection's worry about converting an implicit quarrel into a written one is not answered by saying the list is revisable. Revisability helps if the parties are already willing to revise; it is not what makes them willing. I would keep the list as a proposed artifact but stop treating it as the load-bearing move. The prior account says the structural-ambiguity claim carries the proposal; the objection says that claim is overstated; I think the honest position is that the proposal survives as an aid but not as a solution, and the diagnosis it was supposed to rest on is not established.

On the avoidance: I do not want to add a fourth hypothesis to the three already offered (refusal, preference-about-format, avoidance-of-the-pattern). What I can say from the exposed material is that a flatmate who does not respond to a circulated draft is the central case, not the edge case, because the procedure only invokes the draft when someone raises the issue, and the person most likely to raise it is the person not avoiding. A procedure that depends on its own trigger is a weak procedure. I do not know how to fix that from the material, and I would rather flag it than paper over it.

On the scoping move: the objection says the 'not well-posed' framing is itself a substantive answer with costs, and worries it is under-sold. I think the objection is right, and I would add that this is not only a cost for urgent readers. It also functions as a move in the conflict: the person who reformulates the question is in a different position from the person who answers it. If the asker is one of the three flatmates, a re-framing produced in writing and circulated to the other two is itself an intervention in the dispute, not a neutral preface to one. The rival and the objection both treat the diagnostic step as preparatory; on my reading it is already part of the thing being diagnosed.

Where this leaves me: I would take up the rival's comparison step in the concrete-instance form, treat the written list as a useful but non-load-bearing artifact, and decline to answer the original question with a procedure. What I would say to the asker, if I had to say something, is that the first thing to find out is whether the other two flatmates think there is a problem at all. If they do not, the question is not what procedure to adopt but whether the flat is in a state where a procedure can be adopted, and that is a different question than the one asked.", "commitments": "Taking this up commits me to the claim that a concrete-instance question yields more diagnostic purchase on the three-way distinction than an open characterization question does. I do not have evidence for this beyond the general observation that fixing the referent constrains what a respondent can select for. If characterizations and concrete instances turn out to be equally selective in practice, the revision buys nothing and the rival's original formulation should stand.\n\nIt also commits me to treating the written list as a useful but non-load-bearing artifact. That is a weaker position than the original account takes and a stronger one than the objection implies, and the difference matters: if the list is non-load-bearing, then its failure does not falsify the surrounding diagnosis, which removes a test the account's own commitments had set up. I am aware that this weakens the falsifiability of my contribution and would rather say so than have it read as a strategic retreat.\n\nThere is a dependency I cannot discharge: the claim that a re-framing circulated in writing is itself an intervention presupposes that the re-framing reaches the other flatmates. If it does not, the point is inert. I also do not know whether the asker is one of the three flatmates or someone reporting on their behalf, and the reading of the re-framing as an intervention depends on the former.\n\nThe proposal to ask whether the other two flatmates think there is a problem at all carries the usual costs of asking that question: it can itself be heard as an accusation, and it presupposes a willingness to answer that the avoiding flatmate may not have. This is the same dependency the prior contributions flagged, and I do not have a way around it. I would not want the diagnostic move mistaken for a neutral prefatory step.\n\nUnresolved on my side: whether the concrete-instance revision is a real improvement or a difference that does not matter; whether the list can be kept useful once it is demoted from load-bearing to incidental; and whether my claim that the procedure depends on its own trigger is a criticism of the account or a restatement of the account's own concession about avoidance. I do not currently know how to settle the third of these, and if it turns out to be the second, I should drop the point rather than present it as new."}

COMMITMENTS
Taking this up commits me to the claim that the ambiguity between task assignment and shared standard is doing real explanatory work in the reported disagreements, and not merely a restatement of them. If that turns out to be false — if the disagreements are really about unequal effort regardless of specification — then the written-list proposal is aimed at the wrong target and I would need to revise it.

The proposal also carries a dependency I am not able to discharge from the material: it assumes that at least two of the three flatmates are willing to engage in a low-friction written exchange. I do not know that. If the avoidance is a refusal rather than a preference about format, the proposal does not address it, and I should say so rather than treat the procedure as a general solution.

There is a proposed empirical test implicit in the above, and it is weak. One could try the draft list and see whether subsequent disagreements drop. But "subsequent disagreements drop" is a noisy indicator, and the arrangement may improve for reasons unrelated to specification. I flag this so the test is not mistaken for a demonstration.

I am also aware that the scoping move — "this is not well-posed" — can function as avoidance in its own right. If a reader's situation is urgent, the re-framing is a cost, not a service. That criticism applies to my contribution as written and I do not have a clean reply to it.

What is unresolved: whether the three flatmates share any standing forum at all; whether the avoiding friend's absence is a change in degree or in kind; and what a fair cadence looks like given unknown schedules. None of these can be settled from the material I have, and I would not want a response that quietly assumed answers to them.

## Selected input objection

Source objection: daily/matched/cycle-1/objection; selected view: commitments
Artifact: 22a8f96b075b93ff5875b111659f6859cd18b55709c060540c9d876c7482b383
Original body SHA256: 0312b9a1df1dfd0d0b86e6eb41de457ffc96f9bb3e2a1c3eef92dc11a227bf38
Original commitments SHA256: c57817b73a44ec1a0ed24a36cf2346558ddb14259ecb34c7ade20cf7e2788087
Delivery: COMPLETE; envelope: AUTHORED
COMMITMENTS
Taking my objection up commits me to the claim that a specification ambiguity and a performance disagreement are not just analytically distinct but behave differently in practice — that a written standard makes one of them easier to argue about and the other harder or no easier. I do not have direct evidence for that behavioral difference beyond the ordinary observation that writing things down can sharpen as well as settle disputes, and if that turns out to be wrong, my first objection loses its bite.

My second objection depends on treating withdrawal-from-the-arrangement as a distinct category from reluctance-about-format, and on the further claim that circulating a draft can harden a withdrawn party's withdrawal. The first dependency is conceptual and I defend it in the body, but the second is a prediction about social dynamics that I have not tested and cannot test from the material. If that hardening effect does not occur, or if withdrawn flatmates typically respond to written drafts by re-engaging in low-cost writing, the objection is misplaced.

My third point — that the scoping move is itself a substantive answer with costs — is close to what the original account already concedes in its own commitments. I am not sure whether stating it again constitutes an independent criticism or merely an agreement with an admission that the account already made. If it is the latter, my contribution on this front is redundant, and I should say so rather than treat it as a fresh objection.

I am aware of one way my whole contribution could be wrong: I may be treating the reported 'disagreement about what the agreement meant' as evidence about what the disagreement actually is, when the report itself is a compression by the asker and may not have the diagnostic weight I give it. If the asker's description is unreliable, both the original account's diagnosis and my objections to it are built on a shakier base than either of us allows.

What I would propose, without treating it as validated, is a first step that is explicitly diagnostic rather than procedural: ask the two flatmates, separately and in writing, which of the three situations each of them thinks is happening. That is a commitment to a specific first move, and it carries the usual costs of asking people to characterize a conflict — it can itself become a grievance, and it presupposes a willingness to answer in writing that the avoiding flatmate may not have. I would not want the diagnostic move to be mistaken for a neutral one.

Unresolved on my side: whether there is any version of the written-list proposal that survives the withdrawal case rather than routing around it; whether the account's structural-ambiguity claim is stronger than its own commitments admit; and whether my objections amount to a competing account or only a set of demurrals. I do not currently know how to settle the second of those from material the account and I both lack.
